words.scene: A name written across a newly drawn coastline; someone standing on that land as one of its people.
words.definition_pt: Uma pessoa ou coisa dos Estados Unidos (no Brasil, quase sempre quer dizer isso).
words.parts_meaning: América is named after Amerigo Vespucci; Latin -ānus = "of, from"
words.origin: Vespucci's Latinized name Americus was used for the New World on Waldseemüller's 1507 map. The suffix -ano comes directly from Latin -ānus. Feminine: americana.
culture: In Brazil americano usually means from the US. Some Latin Americans point out that everyone in the Americas is americano, so you'll also hear norte-americano and estadunidense.
notes: Feminine form: americana

words.scene: A finger jabs at the ground at your feet: right here.
words.root_image: Vulgar Latin *accu hīc ≈ "look! here!": a pointing gesture at the ground, built into the word.
words.definition_pt: Neste lugar, perto de mim.
words.parts_meaning: Latin eccum / *accu = "behold"; hīc = "here"
words.origin: Vulgar Latin *accu hīc ("look, here!") → aqui. The emphatic "look" piece fused on.
history: English link: There's no everyday English cognate, but the same Latin "this/here" family appears in ad hoc ("for this").
notes: Three-way "here/there": aqui (here, near me) → aí (there, near you) → ali / lá (over there). E aí? = "What's up?" (lit. "and there?").

words.scene: The body at ease, everything running smoothly, nothing catching.
words.root: Latin bene ‘well’ (deeper origin beyond Old Latin is uncertain)
words.root_image: Latin bene = well, rightly (its adjective is bonus, "good"). There's no clear physical image, and its origin beyond Old Latin is uncertain.
words.definition_pt: De um jeito bom. “Estou bem” = está tudo bom comigo.
words.parts_meaning: "well"
words.origin: Latin bene → bem (final -e lost, n became a nasal vowel). Portuguese keeps a plain e where Spanish breaks it into ie (bien).
history: Why English split: Everyday English well is Germanic. Bene survives only in compounds: benefit ("done well"), benediction ("well-speaking" = blessing), benevolent ("well-wishing").
notes: As a noun: meu bem = "my dear, darling" (very common endearment); bens = goods, assets.

words.scene: A stick of wood glowing like a coal, red dye seeping from it.
words.root: probably Portuguese brasa ‘ember’ (for the red dyewood); not certain
words.definition_pt: O maior país da América do Sul, onde se fala português.
words.parts: bras(a) (ember, glowing coal) + -il (suffix; the exact formation is uncertain)
words.parts_meaning: probably from brasa "ember," for the glowing red dye
words.origin: named after pau-brasil (brazilwood), a red dyewood that was the colony's first major export. Brasil was already a name for red dyewoods in medieval European trade, before 1500. Deriving it from brasa "ember" is the most accepted explanation, but not certain; links to the legendary Atlantic island "Hy-Brasil" have also been proposed. When Pedro Álvares Cabral arrived in 1500, the land was first called Ilha de Vera Cruz, then Terra de Santa Cruz, before Brasil took over.
notes: Portuguese spells it with s; English with z.

words.scene: A merchant with arms full of red dyewood — the one who works that timber.
words.definition_pt: Uma pessoa ou coisa do Brasil (forma masculina).
words.parts: Brasil + -eiro (one who deals with / belongs to)
words.parts_meaning: Brasil (see below); -eiro < Latin -ārius "connected with, one who does"
words.origin: Latin -ārium → -eiro (the i moved forward: -ariu → -airo → -eiro). -eiro normally marks professions (padeiro baker, carpinteiro carpenter). It's often noted that brasileiro originally meant someone who traded brazilwood, which explains why the word isn't the expected brasiliense or brasiliano.
notes: brasiliense = someone from Brasília, the capital.

words.photo_credit: Eugene Pik (Eugenepik) / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Leather_bi-fold_wallet_by_Eugene_Pik_(2021)_04.jpg
words.scene: A leather fold resting on the table, bills and a card tucked inside.
words.root_image: Latin charta (from Greek chartēs) = a sheet of papyrus, a paper, a letter. An -eira is a place or holder for that thing: a paper-holder, a place for documents and bills.
words.definition_pt: Uma coisa pequena para guardar o seu dinheiro.
words.parts_meaning: carta < Latin charta "paper, letter" (from Greek chartēs); -eira = a place or thing that holds that
words.origin: Portuguese carta (letter, paper, charter) + the suffix -eira, which makes a container or place for something. A carteira is originally a holder for papers; it came to mean the wallet you carry, and also certain official documents kept in one.
history: English link: English card, chart, charter, carton, and cartoon all go back to the same Latin / Greek charta, a sheet of paper. Wallet is a different, possibly Germanic word. Portuguese kept the "paper-holder" picture.
culture: In Brazil carteira is the everyday wallet, but the same word is used for official booklets and cards: carteira de motorista (driver's license), carteira de trabalho (the formal work card), carteira de identidade (ID). Context tells you which one.
notes: Feminine: a carteira, uma carteira. Plural: carteiras.

words.scene: You tilt your head, measuring the way a thing is being done.
words.root: Latin quōmodo = quō + modō ‘by what measure’
words.root_image: Latin modus first meant a measure (a measured amount, a rhythm, a limit), then a "way of doing." Quō modō = "by what measure?" → "how?"
words.definition_pt: A palavra que pergunta o jeito ou a forma: “Como vai?”
words.parts_meaning: Latin quōmodo = quō ("in what") + modō ("manner, measure")
words.origin: quōmodo → Vulgar Latin *quomo → como.
history: Why English split: English asks with Germanic how, but the measure root lives on in mode, model ("a small measure"), modest (keeping to measure), moderate, modify.
notes: como also means "as, like" (como eu = like me), and como = "I eat" (from comer, a different Latin word, comedere). Como como? = "How do I eat?"
Homonym: como also means 'I eat' (from comer, a different Latin word).

words.scene: Something coming away from its source.
words.definition_pt: Mostra de onde vem ou de quem é: “de Nova York”, “a mala do senhor”.
words.literal: origin (sou de Nova York), possession (o livro de Zach), material (de madeira)
words.parts_meaning: "down from, away from; about"
words.origin: Latin dē → de.
notes: It merges with articles: de + o = do, de + a = da, de + os = dos, de + as = das.

words.scene: Two fingers held up; a pair of things side by side.
words.root_image: Latin duo = two: a pair, one and one together.
words.definition_pt: O número 2.
words.parts_meaning: dois < Latin duōs, accusative of duo "two"
words.origin: Latin duo → Portuguese dois (masculine) and duas (feminine). The -s is from the accusative duōs. A regular pair like um / uma: dois dólares, duas malas.
history: English link: two is the Germanic cousin of Latin duo (same Indo-European root). English also borrowed the Latin family later: duo, dual, duet, double, dozen (via duodecim, "two and ten").
cognates: English two, duo, dual, duet, double, dozen
notes: dois with masculine nouns (dois dólares, dois reais, dois hotéis). duas with feminine (duas malas, duas carteiras).

words.photo_credit: ESEMES (photograph of a US Treasury note) / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:US_one_dollar_bill,_obverse,_series_2009.jpg
words.scene: A United States one-dollar note, Washington in the center, ONE DOLLAR along the bottom.
words.root: German Thaler, from Joachimsthaler (a coin of Joachimsthal)
words.root_image: Silver coins streaming out of a mountain valley — the valley of Joachim — and traveling the world under a shortened name.
words.definition_pt: O dinheiro dos Estados Unidos. O símbolo é US$.
words.literal: a coin named for Joachim's Valley, shortened and borrowed worldwide
words.parts_meaning: the US (and other) dollar
words.origin: German Thaler, shortened from Joachimsthaler, a silver coin first minted in 1518 in Joachimsthal (today Jáchymov, in the Czech Republic). German Thal / Tal means "valley," so a Joachimsthaler is a coin from Joachim's Valley. The coin and the name spread across Europe (Dutch daalder, Swedish daler, Spanish dólar, and the widely used Spanish dollar or piece of eight). English dollar comes from the same Thaler, famously by way of that Spanish dollar. Portuguese dólar is a later borrowing for the US (and other) dollar.
history: English link: dollar is the same word. No split: Portuguese borrowed the international name.
English link: dollars is the same word in the plural.
culture: The US dollar shows up in Brazilian travel, electronics, and export talk; prices are often compared to o dólar. The Thaler also left a wider mark on coinage (for example the Maria Theresa thaler).
notes: Word history: from German Thaler, from Joachimsthaler (a silver coin of Joachimsthal).

words.scene: Arm draws the bowstring back to the cheek, eyes locked on the mark. Release. Thud. It lands.
words.root_image: Latin tendere = to stretch. Romans used it for drawing a bow (arcum tendere) and for pitching a tent by stretching hides over poles. In-tendere = to stretch toward: pull the string back and aim at a target. Latin applied the same picture to the mind: intendere animum = "aim the mind at" something, strain your attention toward it. Understanding is the arrow landing.
words.definition_pt: Pegar o sentido: a ideia chega na mente.
words.parts_meaning: in- = "toward, into"; tendere = "to stretch"; -e = "he/she/it/you (formal)"
words.origin: Latin intendere, "to stretch toward, aim (the mind) at" → "pay attention to" → "understand." Latin short i → e (in- → en-), and the 3rd-person ending -it reduced to -e (intendit → entende).
history: Same root in English: tension (the stretch), tent (stretched cloth), tendon (the cord stretched across a joint), extend (stretch out), attend (stretch toward = pay attention), pretend (stretch something out in front of you as a screen), tend / tendency (lean in a direction), intense (stretched hard; from intendere itself).

Why English split: English already had a native word for this sense: understand, from Old English understandan (under + standan), recorded well before the Norman Conquest of 1066. Why "stand under" came to mean "grasp" is debated. One theory is that Old English under could mean "among, between" (like German unter), so the word meant to stand in the middle of a matter, but that's uncertain. When Old French entendre came into Middle English, the "understand" slot was taken, so the borrowing survived in its "aiming" sense: intend = aim your will at a goal (intent, intention). English then re-spelled it after the Latin in-.

French took a third path: Old French entendre meant "pay attention to; understand." Over the late Middle Ages and early modern period it narrowed to "hear" (aiming your ears), pushing out the older verb ouïr. French now uses comprendre for "understand." The old sense survives in bien entendu ("of course," lit. "well understood") and in double entendre.

Why Portuguese kept it: Portuguese and Spanish (entender) simply kept the late-Latin meaning "aim the mind → grasp it." No native rival word took over that job, so entender stayed the everyday verb. Portuguese doesn't need an "understand." The bow image is the understanding.

"Intend" is not entender: For "intend" Portuguese uses pretender (Pretendo viajar = I intend to travel). That's a false friend: English "pretend" is fingir in Portuguese. You'll also see tencionar (formal, from tenção "intention," the same tendere root) and ter a intenção de. Related idioms: entender de = to know about (Ele entende de fotografia), entendido = an expert, dar a entender = to hint.
cognates: English intend, attend, extend, tend, tension, tendon
French entendre (now "to hear," but the old "understand" sense survives in bien entendu and double entendre)
notes: As in "O senhor entende português?"

words.scene: Separate posts standing in a row, then bound into a single bundle.
words.root_image: Latin stāre = to stand; status = how something stands, its standing. Ūnus = one, so unidos = "made one."
words.definition_pt: Um país grande da América do Norte. A capital é Washington.
words.parts_meaning: status = "standing, condition," from stāre "to stand"; ūnītus = "made one," from ūnus "one"
words.origin: Latin status → estado (e- added before s + consonant, t → d). ūnītos → unidos (t → d).
history: English link: Here English kept both roots directly: state, status, estate, statue (a standing figure); unite, union, unit. No split.
cognates: English state, status, estate, station, statue
French États-Unis (estat lost its s, marked by the é)
notes: The plural article sticks: os Estados Unidos são...

words.english: to be (for now: state or location)
words.scene: Someone standing on a spot right now; a moment later the spot is empty.
words.root_image: Latin stāre = to stand: where you are standing now, not what you are.
words.definition_pt: Como ou onde uma coisa está agora: “Onde está o hotel?” “Está bem.”
words.parts_meaning: Portuguese puts an e- in front of st- (Latin stāre → estar), as in estado and Estados Unidos.
words.origin: Latin stāre ‘to stand’. Portuguese adds a supporting e- before s + consonant, so stāre → estar.
notes: ser is for what something is (identity, origin); estar is for how or where it is right now.

words.scene: A hand pressed to your own chest.
words.definition_pt: A pessoa que está falando.
words.origin: Latin ego → Vulgar Latin eo → eu (intervocalic g lost).
history: English link: English I (Old English ic) and Latin ego come from the same Indo-European word. English wore it down to one letter, Portuguese to eu.
notes: Portuguese often drops eu because the verb ending already shows the person (entendo = I understand).

words.scene: A courteous hand, a soft voice — the easy manners of someone raised in a close clan.
words.root: Latin gentīlis ‘of the same clan’ (gēns ‘clan’), via Old French gentil
words.root_image: Latin gēns = clan, a Roman extended family sharing a name (the gens Julia was Julius Caesar's clan). Gentīlis = "belonging to a clan," a free, well-born Roman rather than an outsider. Courtly Old French gentil = noble → noble manners → kind.
words.definition_pt: Uma pessoa boa e educada com os outros.
words.parts_meaning: Latin gēns, gentis = "clan, family" (root gen- "birth, kin"); -ilis = adjective suffix
words.origin: Latin gentīlis "of the same clan" → "well-born, noble" (Old French gentil) → "courteous, kind."
history: Why English split: English borrowed the word several times, and each copy froze a different stage: gentile (Church Latin gentiles, "the nations," meaning non-Jews), gentle (noble → mild), genteel (re-borrowed from French, "refined"), and jaunty (also from French gentil). Portuguese kept just one meaning: kind.
cognates: English gentle, gentleman, genteel, gentile, genus, gene, generate, genre, genial
culture: Portuguese gentil means kind, polite, considerate. It's a strong compliment: Você é muito gentil = "That's very kind of you."
gentileza = kindness; por gentileza = a formal "please."

Gentileza gera gentileza ("kindness generates kindness") is a famous Rio motto from the street preacher José Datrino, known as Profeta Gentileza. His murals on a Rio viaduct are now a protected landmark.

words.photo_credit: The Connaught (Flickr) / CC BY-SA 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_connaught_hotel_london_exterior_entrance.jpg
words.scene: A traveler crossing a threshold, received as both guest and host in the same house.
words.root_image: Latin hospes meant both host AND guest, the two sides of the sacred bond between a traveler and the household that took him in. A hospitāle was a guest house. Its deeper origin is often reconstructed as "lord of strangers" (*ghosti-pot-), which is widely cited but uncertain.
words.definition_pt: Um lugar onde as pessoas pagam para dormir quando viajam.
words.parts_meaning: Latin hospes, hospitis = "host / guest"; hospitāle = "guesthouse"
words.origin: Late Latin hospitāle → Old French hostel → French hôtel (the circumflex marks the lost s) → borrowed into Portuguese as hotel. The h is silent and the stress is on the end: o-TÉL. Plural: hotéis.
history: Why English split: English took this root several times, and each borrowing got a different job: hospital (first a shelter for travelers and the needy), hostel and host (via Old French), hotel (later, from modern French hôtel), hospitality, hospice.
cognates: a family of doublets from one Latin word: English hospital, hostel, hotel, host, hospitality, hospice
notes: The h is silent.
Word history: from French hôtel, from Latin hospitāle (hospes, guest/host). A deeper “lord of strangers” origin is often cited but uncertain.

words.scene: People of a windswept northern peninsula; their name later carried across the water to an island.
words.root: Latin Angli (the Angles), probably via medieval French/Occitan + -ēnsis (path likely but not certain)
words.definition_pt: A língua da Inglaterra e dos Estados Unidos. Também: uma pessoa da Inglaterra.
words.parts_meaning: the Angles, a Germanic people from Angeln (the Jutland peninsula in modern northern Germany/Denmark); -ês < Latin -ensis
words.origin: from the Latin Angli. It probably reached Iberian languages through medieval French/Occitan forms like engleis/anglés, which explains the a → e/i shift. That path is likely but not certain. Inglaterra = "land (terra) of the English."
culture: The Brazilian idiom para inglês ver ("for the English to see") means "just for show, a facade." It's usually traced to 19th-century Brazilian laws against the slave trade, passed under British pressure and then not enforced. That origin is widely told but not proven.

words.scene: A body wading forward through a shallow crossing, stride after stride.
words.root: Latin vādere ‘to go, walk’ (the verb ir also uses īre and esse)
words.root_image: Latin vādere = to go, stride forward, often with purpose. It's probably related to vadum, "a ford" (a shallow crossing). English wade is its Germanic cousin.
words.definition_pt: Sair de um lugar para outro.
words.parts: ir < Latin īre ‘to go’; vai, vou, vamos < Latin vādere
words.parts_meaning: "goes"
words.origin: ir is built from three Latin verbs: vādere "to go, walk" gives vou, vai, vamos, vão; īre "to go" gives the infinitive ir; and esse "to be" gives the past fui (so fui = both "I went" and "I was").
history: Why English split: English uses Germanic go. Vādere shows up in invade (stride in), evade (stride out of reach), pervasive (going through everything). English mixes verbs too: went was borrowed from wend. That's like Portuguese ir, which mixes vou/vai (vādere), ir (īre) and fui (esse).
notes: Vai! = "Go!"; Vamos! = "Let's go!"

words.photo_credit: Sandrine Z / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Belber_Suitcase.jpg
words.scene: A traveler's bag in the hand, a pouch ready for the road.
words.root: Old French male ‘bag, pouch’, from Frankish *malha (Germanic)
words.root_image: Frankish *malha, a traveler's bag or pouch. It's Germanic, not Latin.
words.definition_pt: Uma caixa com alça para levar roupa numa viagem.
words.parts_meaning: "bag, pouch"
words.origin: Old French male "bag, pouch" (modern French malle "trunk"), from Frankish *malha, a Germanic word.
history: English link: English mail is the same word: first the mailbag, then the letters inside.
cognates: English mail comes from the same Old French male: the mailbag came first, then the letters inside. Spanish maleta.
notes: porta-malas = car trunk ("carry-bags"). Brazilian slang: ele é um mala = "he's a pain, a bore" (dead weight you have to carry).
Word history: from Old French male (bag, pouch), from Frankish malha — Germanic, not Latin.

words.scene: A path that turns — you were going one way, then a hand stops you and points the other.
words.root_image: Latin magis = more, to a greater degree. The contrast sense grew out of "more than that": you add a turn, a correction, a however.
words.definition_pt: Uma palavra que vira a ideia: “eu quero, mas não tenho.”
words.parts_meaning: mas < Latin magis "more, rather"
words.origin: Latin magis "more" developed a contrastive sense ("rather, but rather") in spoken Latin and became Portuguese mas and Spanish más / pero, French mais, Italian ma. The old "more" meaning in Portuguese is now mais (with an i), a slightly different development of the same Latin word; mas kept the "but" job.
history: Why English split: English but is Germanic. The Latin magis family survived in English as major, majority, majesty, maximum, plus the prefix mag- (magnify, magnificent). French mais is the same word as Portuguese mas, still meaning "but."
cognates: English major, majority, majesty, maximum, magnify
notes: Don't confuse mas ("but") with mais ("more"). They sound similar in some speech, but they are spelled differently and mean different things. Eu tenho dois, mas não é muito vs. eu tenho mais dólares.

words.scene: Your hand closes over something that is yours.
words.definition_pt: Que é de mim: “o meu hotel”, “a minha mala”.
words.literal: "my," agreeing with the thing owned: minha mala (fem.), meu hotel (masc.)
words.parts: single possessive; masculine meu, feminine minha
words.parts_meaning: "my"
words.origin: Latin mea → Old Portuguese mia / mĩa → minha. Nasalization spread from the initial m and later became written nh. Masculine meu < Latin meum.
history: English link: Latin mea/meum and English me/my/mine share the same Indo-European root.
notes: E.g. "minha mala." Masculine form: meu.

words.scene: A packed street, people pressed shoulder to shoulder.
words.root_image: Latin multus = many, much: a multitude, a crowded street.
words.definition_pt: Uma grande quantidade; também “mais que o normal”: muito gentil.
words.literal: muito = very (muito bem) / much, many (muitos amigos)
words.parts_meaning: "much, many, very"
words.origin: Latin multum → muito (-lt- → -it-, the same pattern as noctem → noite).
history: Why English split: For everyday speech English uses the Germanic much (Old English micel, "great, big") and keeps multi- for learned words (multiply, multimedia). Portuguese muito and Spanish mucho are just multum worn down.
notes: It's pronounced with a nasal "ũi" (roughly "MŨY-too") even though there's no tilde. This is a well-known quirk.

words.scene: A cord loops around your wrist and ties you to the person who just helped you.
words.root_image: Latin ligāre = to tie, bind (a ligament ties bone to bone). Ob-ligāre = to tie toward: a rope runs from you to the person who helped you. Roman law defined an obligatio as a legal bond (iuris vinculum), a debt you're tied to.
words.definition_pt: O que um homem diz para agradecer.
words.parts: ob- (toward, against) + brig- (bind; Latin lig-) + -ado (past participle, "-ed")
words.parts_meaning: ob- = "toward, before"; ligāre = "to bind, tie"; -ado < Latin -ātus = "-ed"
words.origin: Latin obligātus, past participle of obligāre "to bind (to someone)." Two regular sound changes: b + l → br (obligare → obrigar), and intervocalic -t- → -d- (-atum → -ado).
history: Why English split: English kept obliged ("much obliged") but thanks with thank, a Germanic word related to think. To thank is, at root, to "think of" someone's kindness. English says "I'll remember you"; Portuguese says "I'm tied to you."
cognates: English oblige, obligation, "much obliged," ligament, ligature, liable, ally, rely (from Latin religare via Old French)
Spanish obligado (but Spanish uses it for "forced," not "thanks")
culture: Saying obrigado literally means "I'm in your debt," like old English "much obliged" or "I'm beholden to you." Spanish and Italian thank by giving grace (gracias, grazie); Portuguese thanks by declaring a debt.
It describes the speaker, so it agrees with the speaker's gender: men say obrigado, women say obrigada, regardless of who they're thanking. In casual speech you'll sometimes hear the gender ignored.
Intensify: Muito obrigado; casual and warm: Obrigadão!
Replies: De nada ("of nothing"), Por nada, Não há de quê ("there's nothing to thank for"), and the very Brazilian Imagina! ("imagine [that you'd owe me]," like "don't mention it").
notes: Feminine form, said by a woman: obrigada

words.scene: Ships slip through a harbor mouth, a doorway from open sea to land.
words.root: Portus Cale ‘harbor of Cale’ + Latin -ēnsis ‘from’ (Cale is uncertain)
words.root_image: Latin portus = harbor, the place where ships pass in from the sea. It's related to porta, "door, gate." Portus Cale was the harbor at the Douro's mouth, a doorway from sea to land.
words.definition_pt: A língua do Brasil e de Portugal. Também: uma pessoa de Portugal.
words.parts_meaning: Portugal < Portus Cale; -ês < Latin -ensis "from, belonging to"
words.origin: Portus Cale (or Portucale) was a Roman-era settlement at the mouth of the Douro river, where Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia are today. Its name spread to the county, then the kingdom. Portus = "harbor." The origin of Cale is uncertain: possibly pre-Roman, and disputed. Latin -ensis → -ês; the final -al of Portugal dropped out of the adjective.
history: English link: port, portal, passport ("pass the port"). Traditionally also opportunity (ob portum, "toward the harbor," like a wind that brings you to port), but that explanation is plausible, not certain.
cognates: the suffix matches English -ese (Portuguese, Japanese), Italian -ese, Spanish -és, French -ais/-ois
notes: The ê is closed and stressed: por-tu-GUÊS. Feminine: portuguesa. Language names are lowercase.

words.scene: Eyes moving over a group, counting one by one: how many are there?
words.root_image: Latin quantus = of what size, how great. The question is about the measure of a group.
words.definition_pt: Pergunta o número: um, dois, muitos?
words.parts_meaning: quantus = "how great, how much"; -os agrees with a masculine plural noun (quantos dólares)
words.origin: Latin quantus → Portuguese quanto (how much, singular) and quantos (how many, masculine plural). Feminine plural: quantas. Intervocalic -nt- stayed, unlike some other clusters.
history: English link: English quantity, quantitative, quantum, and the question-word how much/how many (Germanic how + much). Quantity is the learned Latin cousin; everyday English uses how many.
cognates: French combien (different word) / quant- in quantité
notes: Quantos for masculine plural (quantos dólares, quantos reais). Quantas for feminine (quantas malas). Quanto / quanta for a singular mass or amount.

words.scene: Your own hands stretch toward something and pull it closer.
words.root_image: Latin quaerere = to seek, to go looking, to ask after something. Wanting is the search already aimed at a thing: you are after it.
words.definition_pt: Desejar uma coisa; estender a mão para ela.
words.parts_meaning: querer < Latin quaerere "to seek, ask, inquire"; -o = 1st person singular
words.origin: Latin quaerere "to seek, to ask" became Portuguese querer, and the meaning settled on "to want" (the thing you are seeking). The 1st-person present is eu quero. Related English borrowings kept the older "ask / seek" sense: query, question, quest, inquire, require, acquire.
history: Why English split: English want is Germanic (originally "to be lacking"). The Latin quaerere survived in English as query, question, quest, inquire, require, acquire, exquisite. Portuguese kept the verb as the everyday word for "to want."
English link: Same split as eu quero: English want is Germanic; query, question, quest keep the Latin seeking root.
cognates: English query, question, quest, inquire, require, acquire
notes: Eu quero um hotel = I want a hotel. Followed by a noun, or by an infinitive in later lessons (eu quero ir).

words.scene: A Brazilian one-real note, the word REAL under the republic's laurel-crowned head.
words.root_image: A king's title stamped on a coin: money that is "royal."
words.definition_pt: O dinheiro do Brasil. O símbolo é R$.
words.parts_meaning: o < Latin illum "that one"; real < Latin rēgālis "royal," from rēx, rēgis "king"
words.origin: Portuguese and Brazilian money have been called real ("the royal one") for centuries. The old plural was réis (as in mil-réis). After a string of 20th-century currencies (cruzeiro, cruzado, cruzeiro real), the modern real was introduced on July 1, 1994, under the Plano Real, the stabilization plan that ended Brazil's hyperinflation. One real = 100 centavos. The modern plural is reais, not réis. Symbol: R$.
history: English link: regal and royal are the same Latin word. English real ("actual") is a look-alike from realis, not rēgālis.
English link: same as o real: regal, royal. English has no everyday plural of this currency name in common use; Portuguese does: reais.
cognates: Spanish real (the old silver coin, and "royal"). Portuguese also has a look-alike real meaning "actual, real," from a different Latin word, realis ("of a thing," from rēs). The currency is the royal word, not the "actual" one. English real ("actual") is that second root.
same as o real: royal, regal
the old Portuguese réis (a different plural of the same word)
culture: The Plano Real (1994), associated with finance minister (later president) Fernando Henrique Cardoso, replaced the cruzeiro real and anchored prices to a new unit. Later note series feature Brazilian animals; the 20-reais note's golden lion tamarin is one example.
notes: Introduced with the Plano Real in 1994. Plural: reais. Symbol: R$.
In much of Brazil the initial r of real sounds like English h: "hey-AL."
Word history: from Latin rēgālis (royal).

words.scene: A worn body sitting down to a meal and feeling itself rebuilt.
words.root: French restaurant ← Latin re- + restaurāre ‘to restore, rebuild’ (deeper root of -staurāre is uncertain)
words.root_image: Latin restaurāre = to rebuild, renew, repair something worn down, like a temple or a wall. In 18th-century Paris a restaurant was a restorative broth, then the shop that sold it.
words.definition_pt: Um lugar onde as pessoas comem e pagam pela comida.
words.parts: o (the) + re- (again, back) + staur- (make firm, restore) + -ante (present participle "-ing")
words.parts_meaning: Latin restaurāre = "to restore, rebuild"; the root of -staurāre is uncertain; -ante = "-ing"
words.origin: French restaurant, "restoring," was first a restorative broth. In the 1760s–70s it came to mean the Paris eating-houses that served such food, and the word spread worldwide, Portuguese included.
history: English link: English uses the root both ways, restore and restaurant. No split, just a French detour. Portuguese restaurar still means to restore (restaurar um quadro = restore a painting).
notes: The initial r sounds like English h.
The initial r sounds like English h: "hes-tau-RAN-chee" (in much of Brazil, -te sounds like "chee").
Word history: from French restaurant, from Latin restaurāre (to restore, rebuild). The deeper root of -staurāre is uncertain.

words.scene: The flavor lands on the tongue; your eyes light up — you have it.
words.root_image: The same tasting root as sei: the flavor is there this time. You have sampled it, and you know.
words.definition_pt: Ter a informação na cabeça.
words.parts_meaning: sabe is the 3rd-person present of saber. você takes 3rd-person verbs because it comes from Vossa Mercê, "Your Grace."
words.origin: the same Latin sapere "to taste" → "to know," as in eu não sei. The 3rd-person sabe is the regular present of saber.
history: English link: Same split as eu não sei: English know is Germanic; savor / sapient / sapiens keep the Latin root.
cognates: same family as eu não sei: savor, sapient, sapiens
pt_family: saber de cor (to know by heart)

words.english: sir, mister; with o / a: the polite “you”
words.scene: An elder with white hair; the room quiets and makes space.
words.root_image: Latin senex = old man; senior = "the older one." Picture the Roman senatus, literally the council of old men: the elders who sat in judgment. In feudal Latin, senior was the lord a vassal served, the elder who protects and commands.
words.definition_pt: Homem, quase sempre mais velho. Com o artigo é a forma educada de dizer “você”: o senhor (homem), a senhora (mulher).
words.parts_meaning: o = "the"; senior = "older," from senex "old" + comparative -ior
words.origin: Latin seniōrem ("the older one") became senhor: -ni- → -nh-. In late and medieval Latin, senior became a title for a lord or feudal superior. The article o comes from Latin illum ("that one"); Portuguese dropped the initial l-.
history: Why English split: English kept this word too, just worn down: senior → Old French sire → English sire and sir. So "Yes, sir" and "Sim, senhor" are the same word. English also re-borrowed senior straight from Latin for "older" (senior citizen), along with senate and senile.
cognates: English senior, senate, senile, sir, sire, monsieur
culture: o senhor / a senhora vs você
In Brazil, the formal "you" is literally "the gentleman / the lady," so the verb is 3rd person: O senhor entende? = "Does the gentleman understand?"
Use it with older people, strangers in service situations, clients, and anyone you want to show respect to. Pimsleur leans on it because it's always safe.
In some families and regions (common in the interior and the Northeast), children call their parents o senhor / a senhora.
Sim, senhor! / Não, senhora! add emphasis or deference.
Senhor also means "Lord" in prayer, and Nossa Senhora is "Our Lady" (the Virgin Mary). The everyday exclamation Nossa! ("Wow!") is short for Nossa Senhora!
Rough scale: o senhor / a senhora (respectful) → você (normal, neutral) → tu (intimate; used regionally, see você).

words.scene: A hand pressed to your chest as you sit firmly planted — not just where you happen to stand, but who you are.
words.root: Latin sum ‘I am’; the infinitive ser blends esse ‘to be’ and sedēre ‘to sit’
words.root_image: ser is built from two Latin verbs: esse "to be" (sou, é, são) and sedēre "to sit" (the infinitive ser, Old Portuguese seer). A memory aid, not etymology: what you are is where you're seated.
words.definition_pt: Dizer quem ou o que uma coisa é: “Eu sou americano.” “Ele é brasileiro.”
words.parts: ser < Latin esse ‘to be’ + sedēre ‘to sit’; sou < sum; é < est
words.parts_meaning: sou = 1st person present of ser "to be"
words.origin: sou comes from Latin sum "I am" (Old Portuguese som; sou became standard later). The verb ser blends two Latin verbs: esse "to be" (which gave sou, é, são) and sedēre "to sit" (which gave the infinitive ser, Old Portuguese seer).
history: Why English split: English has the same ancient roots but keeps them as separate verbs: is shares its source with Latin est, and sit is the Germanic cousin of sedēre. Portuguese merged them into one verb.
pt_family: estar (to be: state or location right now)
notes: ser is for what something is (identity, origin). estar is for state and location (see onde está? in Lesson 4).

words.scene: Something held out toward the other person: this belongs to them.
words.root: Latin suus ‘his, her, its, their own’
words.root_image: Latin suus = one's own, belonging to the person already in view — not to me, to them.
words.definition_pt: De você (ou dele, dela): “o seu hotel”, “a sua carteira”.
words.parts: single possessive; masculine seu, feminine sua
words.parts_meaning: sua < Latin sua, feminine of suus "his/her/its/their own"
words.origin: Latin suus, sua, suum was a reflexive possessive ("one's own"). In Portuguese, seu / sua is used for você (and for ele / ela): a sua carteira = your wallet, because você takes 3rd-person forms. Masculine: seu. Plural: seus / suas.
history: Why English split: English your is a 2nd-person word (related to you). Portuguese sua is historically "his/her/its own" (Latin suus), reused for você because você comes from "Your Grace" and still behaves like a 3rd person. English possessive her/his/its and the learned form sui- (suicide, "of oneself") keep parts of that Latin family.
notes: Agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: a sua carteira, o seu hotel, a sua mala. Used with você (and with ele / ela).

words.scene: Your own hands close around something and keep it.
words.root_image: The same holding image as você tem, now from your own side: your hands, your grip.
words.definition_pt: Segurar uma coisa com você; ela é sua.
words.parts: ter < Latin tenēre ‘to hold’ (tenho < teneō, tem < tenet)
words.parts_meaning: -o = 1st person singular; tenho is "I have"
words.origin: the same Latin tenēre "to hold." The 1st-person present tenho shows the palatal -nh- that developed in this verb (Latin tenēō).
history: English link: Same split as você tem: English have is Germanic; tenacious, tenure, tenant keep the Latin root.

Why English split: English have is Germanic (related to heft). The Latin root survived in tenacious (holding tight), tenure (the holding of an office or land), tenant (one who holds land), retain, contain, maintain, and tenet (a belief you hold).
cognates: English tenacious, tenure, tenant, retain, contain, maintain, tenet, lieutenant

words.scene: One finger held up; a single thing resting in the palm.
words.root_image: Latin ūnus = one, a single thing, not two.
words.definition_pt: O número 1. Também: “um hotel” = qualquer hotel, não um hotel específico.
words.parts_meaning: "one" and also "a / an"
words.origin: Latin ūnus, ūnum "one." Portuguese um is both the number "one" and the indefinite article "a / an," just as English a / an comes from one (an was originally the same word as one). The -n of ūnum nasalized the vowel and then dropped as a consonant, leaving um. Feminine uma < Latin ūnam.
history: English link: one is the Germanic cousin of ūnus. English later re-borrowed the Latin family: unit, unique, union, unanimous, universe. The indefinite article a / an is historically the same word as one, worn down.
English link: same as um: one, a / an, unit, unique.
cognates: English one, an, unit, unique, union, unanimous, universe, onion (from ūniō, "oneness," then a single onion)
Italian un / una (French une is a look-alike; the Portuguese feminine is uma)

words.scene: An old formal bow, worn down by years into a casual nod, still aimed at the other person, not at yourself.
words.root: Vossa Mercê ‘Your Grace’ ← Latin vostra + mercēdem ‘reward, favor’
words.root_image: Latin mercēs = pay, wages, related to merx "merchandise" (market, merchant, commerce). Church Latin used it for the reward God grants, which became "grace, mercy." Vossa Mercê = "Your Grace / Your Favor."
words.definition_pt: A pessoa com quem eu falo, no jeito normal, não formal.
words.parts: contraction of Vossa Mercê ("Your Grace / Your Mercy")
words.parts_meaning: vossa < Latin vostra "your (plural/honorific)"; mercê < Latin mercēdem "wages, reward" → "favor, grace"
words.origin: an honorific worn down by centuries of use: vossa mercê → vossemecê → vosmecê → você → colloquial ocê → cê. Because it was originally "Your Grace," it takes a 3rd-person verb: você é.
history: Why English split: English mercy kept the "compassion" sense, and French merci became "thank you." English "Your Grace" is the exact equivalent of vossa mercê, but English kept it for dukes and archbishops and never wore it down into an everyday "you."
cognates: English mercy, mercenary, merchant share the merc- "pay, trade" root
Spanish usted comes from vuestra merced, the exact same idea.
culture: In most of Brazil, você is the normal, neutral "you" for friends, peers, and strangers your age.
Tu is common in some regions (Rio Grande do Sul, parts of the Northeast, Pará, and casually in Rio), often with a 3rd-person verb (tu vai), which is grammatically "wrong" but normal speech.
In Portugal, você can sound distant or even slightly rude, and tu is the informal norm. This is a generalization; usage varies.
Scale: o senhor / a senhora → você → tu.

forms.definition_pt: Uma pessoa ou coisa do Brasil (forma feminina).
forms.literal: "Brazilian woman" or a feminine noun (a música brasileira)

forms.label: contraction · de + os (masc. plural)
forms.scene: Several things coming away from a group, down from that source.
forms.definition_pt: De + os: “Eu sou dos Estados Unidos.”
forms.origin: de + os fused into one word. Portuguese merges prepositions with articles all the time (do, da, no, na, pelo).
notes: Contraction of de + os (masc. plural). E.g. "dos Estados Unidos."
Many countries take an article: o Brasil → do Brasil; os Estados Unidos → dos Estados Unidos. But Portugal has none: de Portugal.

forms.definition_pt: Mais de um dólar: “vinte dólares”.
forms.root_image: The same valley silver, now a sheaf of notes in the hand.
forms.origin: the same German Thaler / Joachimsthaler name, in the Portuguese plural. Regular -es plural after a consonant-final loan: dólar → dólares (the accent stays on the same syllable, written on the ó).
notes: Word history: from German Thaler, from Joachimsthaler (a silver coin of Joachimsthal).

forms.definition_pt: Eu pego o sentido: a ideia chegou na minha mente.
forms.parts_meaning: -o = 1st person singular, same as in Latin (intendo)
forms.origin: same as entende. The Latin first-person -o survived unchanged; the same thing happened in Spanish and Italian (entiendo, intendo).

forms.definition_pt: O que eu digo para ter uma coisa: “Eu quero a mala.”

forms.scene: The other person's hands stretch toward it, reaching.
forms.definition_pt: Pergunta, ou diz, se a outra pessoa quer uma coisa.
forms.root_image: The same seeking root as eu quero, now on the other side: their hands going after the thing.
forms.parts_meaning: quer is the 3rd-person present of querer; você takes 3rd-person verbs because it comes from Vossa Mercê, "Your Grace."
forms.origin: The same Latin quaerere → querer as in eu quero. The 3rd-person present quer is used with você: você quer?

forms.photo_credit: Oleg Yunakov / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20_Brazilian_Real_banknote_featuring_a_Golden_Lion_Tamarin_monkey.jpg
forms.scene: A Brazilian twenty-reais note, a golden lion tamarin on a branch, the words VINTE REAIS along the edge.
forms.definition_pt: Mais de um real: “vinte reais”.
forms.root_image: The same royal stamp, now on more than one coin or note.
forms.literal: "royal ones" → the modern plural of the currency
forms.parts_meaning: the modern plural of o real
forms.origin: same Latin rēgālis "royal." The historical plural of the old real was réis, which was also the name of the currency for a long time (the réis / mil-réis). After 1994 the official plural is reais.
notes: Pronounced roughly "hey-ICE" in much of Brazil (initial r like English h).
Word history: from Latin rēgālis (royal).

forms.definition_pt: Pergunta ou diz que a outra pessoa tem a informação: “Você sabe onde fica?”

forms.definition_pt: A forma educada de dizer “você” para um homem, quase sempre mais velho.

forms.definition_pt: A forma educada de dizer “você” para uma mulher, quase sempre mais velha.
forms.root: feminine of senhor ← Latin seniōrem ‘the older one’
forms.literal: "the elder lady" → respectful "you" for a woman
forms.parts_meaning: a < Latin illam ("that one," fem.); -a marks feminine
forms.origin: a feminine form of senhor. Latin had no special feminine of senior; Romance built one: Spanish señora, Italian signora, French madame uses a different root (ma dame < mea domina).

forms.label: eu · I am
forms.definition_pt: O que eu digo para falar quem ou o que eu sou: “Eu sou americano.”
forms.literal: "I am" for identity, origin, profession. Eu sou americano. Eu sou fotógrafo.

forms.scene: A stone set in the earth, simply there, by its nature.
forms.definition_pt: Forma do verbo ser: “Ele é brasileiro.” “Você é americano.”
forms.parts: single verb form (3rd person singular of ser)
forms.origin: Latin est → é (final -st lost). "They are" = são < Latin sunt (final -nt → nasal -ão).
notes: "They are" is são.
The accent matters: é (open "eh") = "is"; e (no accent, "ee") = "and."

forms.scene: That same nod, then a quiet naming of who they are, as if speaking of someone a step apart from you.
forms.definition_pt: Forma do verbo ser para “você”: “Você é brasileiro?”

forms.scene: Your hands close around something and keep it.
forms.definition_pt: Pergunta ou diz que a outra pessoa tem alguma coisa: “Você tem uma mala?”
forms.root_image: Latin tenēre = to hold, to keep in the hand and not let go. To have something is, at root, to hold it.
forms.parts_meaning: tem is the 3rd-person present of ter, "to have"; você again takes the 3rd person.
forms.origin: Latin tenēre "to hold, keep" became Portuguese ter. In classical Latin, habēre was the main verb for "to have," and tenēre was "to hold." Spanish still uses both (tener for possession, haber as auxiliary and existential). Older Portuguese also used haver for possession; over time ter took over "to have / to possess," and haver shrank mainly to the existential há ("there is") and some auxiliary uses (havia, haver de).

forms.label: feminine
forms.definition_pt: O número 1 com palavra feminina: “uma mala”.
forms.root_image: The same single thing as um, now agreeing with a feminine noun.
forms.parts_meaning: "one" and also "a / an," agreeing with a feminine noun (uma mala, uma senhora)
forms.origin: Latin ūnam, the feminine of ūnus, became uma. Masculine um < ūnum.

phrases.scene: You part on a path and point back to the same spot, to meet there again soon.
phrases.root: até possibly Arabic ḥattā ‘until’ (disputed); logo ← Latin locō ‘on the spot’
phrases.root_image: logo is Latin locō, "in the place": right on the spot. "On the spot" → "immediately" → "soon." English makes the same move when it says "I'll do it on the spot."
phrases.definition_pt: O que se diz quando vai embora e espera ver a pessoa de novo.
phrases.parts_meaning: até = "until, up to; even"; logo < Latin locō "in the place"
phrases.origin: logo: Latin locō ("on the spot") → "immediately" → "soon." até: disputed. It's often traced to Arabic ḥattā "until" (also proposed for Spanish hasta), a legacy of centuries of Arabic presence in Iberia. Latin sources have also been proposed.
cognates: locō: English local, location, locomotive, locus
pt_family: até já (see you in a moment)
culture: Até logo is a friendly, neutral goodbye and doesn't have to mean the same day.
Family: até amanhã (until tomorrow), até mais (until later), até já (see you in a moment, more common in Portugal).
The most common casual Brazilian goodbye is tchau, from Italian ciao, which comes from Venetian s-ciao "(I am your) slave," originally a deferential greeting, from Latin sclavus.
Logo also means "therefore": Penso, logo existo = "I think, therefore I am."
notes: até has no confirmed Latin image. Arabic ḥattā "until" is the leading theory, but it's disputed.

phrases.scene: Darkness settles; a quiet greeting as the sky goes black.
phrases.definition_pt: O que se diz para cumprimentar ou para ir embora, à noite.
phrases.parts_meaning: noite < Latin noctem
phrases.origin: noctem → noite (-ct- → -it-, the signature Portuguese change; Spanish has noche).
history: English link: A true cognate: Latin noctem and English night come from the same Indo-European word. Also nocturnal and equinox ("equal night").
cognates: English night (Germanic relative), nocturnal, nocturne, equinox
culture: Unlike English, one phrase covers both "good evening" (arriving at 8 pm dinner) and "good night" (leaving or going to bed). Switch from boa tarde at dusk.

phrases.scene: The sun hangs lower, the air slows; you greet someone in the late light.
phrases.root_image: Latin tardus = slow, sluggish, late. As a memory aid (not etymology), the afternoon is the slow, late stretch of the day as the sun drags toward evening.
phrases.definition_pt: O que se diz para cumprimentar depois do almoço, até a noite.
phrases.parts_meaning: boa < Latin bona; tarde < Latin tardē "late, slowly"
phrases.origin: bona → boa (intervocalic n dropped). The adverb tardē ("late") became a noun meaning "the late part of the day."
history: English link: tardy (late to class); retard originally meant "to slow down"; ritardando in music = slowing.
notes: tarde is feminine, so it's boa. As an adverb it still means "late": É tarde = "It's late." Use it from noon to dusk.

phrases.scene: Morning light floods the sky; you greet someone under the brightness.
phrases.root: Latin bonum + diēs ‘day’ (from a root ‘to shine’)
phrases.root_image: Latin diēs comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to shine," the bright sky. The same root gives Latin deus (god) and divine, Iuppiter (from "sky-father"), and Greek Zeus. A day is "the bright sky."
phrases.definition_pt: O que se diz para cumprimentar de manhã, até o almoço.
phrases.parts_meaning: bom < Latin bonum; dia < Latin diēs "day"
phrases.origin: bonum → bom (final -n became a nasal vowel); feminine boa < bona (intervocalic n dropped). Latin diēs → Vulgar Latin dia.
history: Why English split: English day looks like dia but is NOT related: it's Germanic, from a different root. English uses diēs only in learned words: diary, diurnal, meridian ("midday"), and via French journal and journey (originally a day's travel).
cognates: diary, dial, diurnal, meridian, and journal (via diurnalis)
French bonjour and Italian buongiorno (both use diurnum for "day")
culture: greetings by time of day
Bom dia: from waking up until about noon or lunch.
Boa tarde: from noon until dusk (roughly 6 pm).
Boa noite: after dark, both as "good evening" when arriving and "good night" when leaving.
Brazilians greet a room, a shop, or an elevator with these. Walking into a store without a bom dia can seem a bit cold.
notes: dia is masculine despite the -a (o dia), so it's bom dia, not boa dia.

phrases.scene: You pause in a doorway and wait for a nod before stepping through.
phrases.root_image: Latin licet = "it is allowed," a word from law and custom rather than a physical picture. Licentia = the freedom to act, a granted allowance. No concrete original image is known.
phrases.definition_pt: O que se diz, com educação, antes de passar, entrar ou interromper.
phrases.parts_meaning: cum = "with"; licentia = "freedom, permission," from licēre "to be allowed" + -entia (abstract noun "-ence")
phrases.origin: Latin licentia → licença (-tia → -ça, the same shift as -tion → -ção). Cum → com.
history: Why English split: English license took the official-permit sense (driver's license), and licentious took the "too much freedom" sense. For the polite phrase, English says excuse me, from Latin ex + causa ("out of the charge/accusation"). English asks to be let off the blame, often after the fact. Portuguese asks for permission before acting.
cognates: English license, licit, illicit, leisure (via Old French loisir < licēre), prefix com-/con- (combine, connect)
culture: It's literally a request for a license to act: to get past someone, step into a room or someone's home, interrupt, leave the table, or take something.
It's said before the action. Desculpa / desculpe ("sorry") is said after you bump into someone or make a mistake.
You'll often hear just Licença! in a crowded bus or market.

Common replies: Pois não ("of course / go ahead"), Fique à vontade ("make yourself comfortable"). A playful Brazilian reply is Toda! ("all of it," meaning you have all the permission you need). That one is informal.

phrases.english: how are you? (formal, to a woman)
phrases.scene: The elder woman walks in; you watch how her steps are going, and the room makes space.
phrases.root: Latin quōmodo + vādere + feminine of seniōrem
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta educada para uma mulher, quase sempre mais velha: como ela está.
phrases.literal: a respectful greeting to a woman, especially an older one
phrases.parts_meaning: "how goes the lady?"
phrases.origin: see components.

phrases.english: how are you? (formal, to a man)
phrases.scene: The white-haired elder walks in; you watch how his steps are going, and the room makes space.
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta educada para um homem, quase sempre mais velho: como ele está.
phrases.literal: the respectful version of como vai?. The verb stays 3rd person because you're grammatically talking about "the gentleman."
phrases.parts_meaning: "how goes the gentleman?"
phrases.origin: see components.
culture: Use it with an older man, a hotel manager, a client.
notes: Literally "how goes it, sir?"

phrases.scene: You watch the other person's stride, still from a slight formal distance.
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta normal, não formal: como a outra pessoa está.
phrases.literal: a friendly como vai?. Answer: Vou bem, e você?
phrases.parts_meaning: "how goes you (Your Grace)?"
phrases.origin: see components.

phrases.scene: Someone walks toward you; you watch the pace and the set of their shoulders.
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta comum quando encontra alguém: como a pessoa está.
phrases.parts_meaning: "how goes (it)?"
phrases.origin: see como and vai.
pt_family: como vai você? (how are you?, informal)
culture: It's a bit more polite or classic than Tudo bem?. Typical answer: Vou bem, obrigado, e você? ("I go well, thanks, and you?") or just Bem, obrigado.
notes: Literally "how goes it?"

phrases.scene: Stepping away from a vast harbor city of towers.
phrases.root: Latin dē + nova + York (Old English Eoforwīc ← Latin Eboracum ← Celtic, probably ‘place of yews’)
phrases.definition_pt: Que vem da cidade de Nova York.
phrases.parts_meaning: nova < Latin nova (fem. of novus "new")
phrases.origin: nova kept its Latin form. Portuguese doesn't break the o into ue the way Spanish does (Nueva York). York goes back to Old English Eoforwīc, from Latin Eboracum, from a Celtic name probably meaning "place of yews." New York was named in 1664 for the Duke of York (later James II).
history: English link: Latin novus and English new are true cognates. A nova is a "new" star.
cognates: English novel, novice, innovate, renovate, nova
notes: Brazilian spelling is Nova York; Nova Iorque is the Portugal/standard spelling. de novo = "again."

phrases.scene: You turn and look back down the road, to the place someone came from.
phrases.root_image: Latin unde = "from which place, whence": looking back down the road someone came by.
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta o lugar de origem: “De onde você é?”
phrases.parts_meaning: onde < Latin unde "from where, whence"
phrases.origin: Latin unde meant "from where," but in Portuguese onde drifted to plain "where." So Portuguese added de again: de onde is historically "from from-where." Spanish donde is itself de + unde fused, which makes ¿de dónde? a double-double.
history: Why English split: English has its own whence (Germanic), but it's archaic, so English says "from where." Portuguese onde lost its "from" meaning, so it needed de again.
notes: De onde você é? = "Where are you from?" Also aonde = "to where" (a + onde).

phrases.scene: Almost nothing in the palm — far too little.
phrases.root_image: est = it is; multum here is "very," turning the smallness up; paucum = little, a pinch. The amount is not just small — it is very small.
phrases.definition_pt: É uma quantidade muito pequena.
phrases.parts_meaning: é < est; muito here is the adverb "very"; pouco < Latin paucum "few, little" (already in um pouco)
phrases.origin: pouco < paucum (au → ou). muito before an adjective or adverb means "very" (muito pouco, muito bem, muito gentil). So é muito pouco is stronger than é pouco: it's very little.
history: English link: little and few are Germanic. Latin paucus survived in English as paucity and in the music term poco. The same muito that means "much" also does the job of English very.
notes: muito here means "very," not "a lot of": muito pouco = very little.

phrases.scene: A nod, shoulders settling — everything stands all right where it is.
phrases.root_image: stāre = to stand, to be in a place or state right now; bene = well. The situation stands well — it is all right.
phrases.definition_pt: Tudo está certo, sem problema. Também: “ok.”
phrases.parts_meaning: está < Latin stat, from stāre "to stand"; bem < Latin bene "well"
phrases.origin: The same estar < stāre already in onde está?, plus bem < bene (already in bem, muito bem, tudo bem). Together they mean the state is good: está bem = "it's okay / all right." In speech está often shortens to tá: tá bem.
history: English link: English stand is the Germanic cousin of stāre; well is Germanic too. English okay / all right covers the same job. Portuguese describes the state as standing well.
notes: In speech, está is often tá: Tá bem. Close in meaning to tudo bem, but está bem can also answer a request: "Is that all right?" — Está bem.

phrases.scene: You taste and find nothing — a slow shake of the head, empty hands.
phrases.root_image: Latin sapere = to taste, to have flavor. Taste is the first test of what is in front of you: bitter or sweet, sound or spoiled. From that bodily judgment came "to have discernment," then "to know, to be wise." Homo sapiens is literally "the tasting / wise human." Latin nōn is simply "not," the same particle that English keeps in non-.
phrases.definition_pt: O que eu digo quando a resposta não está na minha cabeça.
phrases.parts_meaning: eu < Latin ego; não < Latin nōn "not"; sei is the irregular 1st-person present of saber, "to know"
phrases.origin: Latin nōn became Portuguese não (the tilde marks a nasal vowel). sei belongs to saber, from Latin sapere "to taste, to have flavor." That physical sense developed a mental one: to have discernment, to be wise, to know. The 1st-person present is irregular: eu sei, not *sabo (compare Spanish sé, French sais, Italian so).
history: Why English split: English know is Germanic (related to can, cunning, and ken). The Latin root survived in English as savor (taste), sapient and sage (wise), insipid ("without taste"), and sapiens.
cognates: English savor, sapient, sage, insipid, Homo sapiens
French savoir / je ne sais pas

phrases.scene: You point into the distance, to a spot already fixed in place, over there.
phrases.root: fīgere ‘to fix’ + Latin illāc ‘that way, over there’
phrases.root_image: lá < Latin illāc, "that way, over there."
phrases.definition_pt: Está naquele lugar, longe de nós: “O hotel fica lá.”
phrases.parts_meaning: lá < Latin illāc "that way, over there"
phrases.origin: illāc → lá (initial il- dropped, like illum → o).
culture: lá is everywhere in casual speech. Sei lá (lit. "I know there") = "who knows / no idea," often with a shrug.

phrases.scene: A teacher's hands open wide, a deep nod, again and again.
phrases.definition_pt: Bem de verdade. Também se diz para elogiar: “Muito bem!”
phrases.parts_meaning: see muito and bem
phrases.origin: Latin multum bene.
notes: It's also praise, "Well done!", the way a teacher would say it. Estou muito bem = "I'm very well."

phrases.scene: The binding cord of thanks pulled tighter, a deeper bow.
phrases.root_image: The same binding as obrigado: a cord looping around the wrist, tying you to the person who helped you — pulled tighter this time, with more of you in the knot.
phrases.definition_pt: Obrigado, com mais força: o que um homem diz quando alguém é muito gentil.
phrases.parts: muito (very, much) + obrigado (obliged, thank you — said by a man)
phrases.parts_meaning: muito < multum "much, very"; obrigado < Latin obligātus "bound, obliged" (ob- + ligāre "to bind")
phrases.origin: The everyday obrigado / obrigada of Lesson 2, intensified with muito. A man says muito obrigado; a woman says muito obrigada. The phrase is the Portuguese equivalent of English much obliged, and it is built of the same Latin pieces (multum + obligātus), even though everyday English now prefers thank you very much.
history: English link: much obliged is the exact English cousin, now a bit old-fashioned; thank you very much uses Germanic thank. The Latin pieces are still visible in obliged / obligation. Portuguese just says the everyday words: muito obrigado.
cognates: Spanish muy obligado (rare; usually muchas gracias)
pt_family: obrigado (thank you, said by a man)
obrigada (thank you, said by a woman)
notes: Said by a man. A woman says muito obrigada. Replies: de nada, por nada, imagina, não há de quê.

phrases.scene: A warm, easy smile spreading as you meet someone, like a pleasant taste.
phrases.root_image: Latin placēre = to please, be agreeable. It's often linked to placāre (to calm, soothe), but the deeper image behind the root is uncertain.
phrases.definition_pt: O que se diz quando conhece uma pessoa pela primeira vez.
phrases.parts: muito (much) + praz- (please) + -er (infinitive, used as a noun)
phrases.parts_meaning: prazer < Latin placēre "to please"; the infinitive works as a noun ("pleasure")
phrases.origin: placēre → prazer. Two regular changes: pl → pr (consonant + l → r) and intervocalic c → z (like facere → fazer, dicere → dizer).
history: Why English split: English kept please and pleasure, but for introductions it says "nice to meet you." Nice comes from Latin nescius ("not knowing, ignorant") and meant "foolish" in Middle English before softening to "pleasant." Portuguese just says "much pleasure."
cognates: English please, pleasure, placid, complacent, placebo ("I will please")
Italian piacere (also how Italians say "nice to meet you")
pt_family: o prazer é meu (the pleasure is mine)
culture: Said when you're introduced. Replies: O prazer é meu ("the pleasure is mine") or Igualmente ("likewise").

It often comes with a handshake. In social settings Brazilians, especially women, greet with cheek kisses; the number varies by region and person (often one in São Paulo, two in Rio), so follow the other person's lead.
Just Prazer! works casually.
notes: Literally "much pleasure."

phrases.scene: A thick sheaf of dollar notes filling the hands.
phrases.root_image: multus = many, a packed crowd; the dollar's name is the Thaler, a coin from Joachim's Valley, now in a thick stack.
phrases.definition_pt: Uma grande quantidade de dólares.
phrases.parts_meaning: muitos is the masculine plural of muito < Latin multum; dólares is the plural of dólar, from German Thaler
phrases.origin: muito agrees in number and gender: muito (adv.), muita, muitos, muitas. With dólares (masculine plural) it is muitos dólares. The noun dólar is the same Thaler / Joachimsthaler borrowing as in Lesson 5.
history: English link: many is Germanic; multi- keeps the Latin root. dollar and dólar are the same Thaler word.
cognates: English many dollars (Germanic many + the same dollar)
notes: muitos agrees with dólares (masc. pl.). Feminine would be muitas.

phrases.scene: Fingers opening a wallet; the money is inside it, in their fold.
phrases.root_image: in = in, inside; a + sua mark the wallet as hers/yours; the wallet itself is the paper-holder. The whole picture is: inside the fold that belongs to the other person.
phrases.definition_pt: Dentro da carteira de você.
phrases.parts: na (in the, fem.) + sua (your, fem.) + carteira (wallet)
phrases.parts_meaning: na = em + a (in + the, feminine); sua = your (fem.); carteira = wallet
phrases.origin: na is the regular contraction of em + a, the same pattern as no = em + o. sua agrees with carteira (feminine). The three pieces fuse into one everyday phrase: na sua carteira.
history: English link: English in is the Germanic cousin of Latin in. English has no everyday contraction like na (in + the). The possessive, as with sua, is a 3rd-person form used for você.
cognates: Spanish en tu cartera / en su cartera
notes: na = em + a. With a masculine noun it would be no (no hotel). sua agrees with carteira.

phrases.scene: Looking at a small amount and shaking the head: that isn't a lot.
phrases.root_image: nōn = not; est = it is; multum = much. The amount standing in front of you is not a large one.
phrases.definition_pt: Não é uma quantidade grande.
phrases.parts_meaning: não < nōn; é < Latin est "is"; muito < multum
phrases.origin: A whole-clause version of não muito: é (from Latin est, already in Lesson 1) sits in the middle, so the phrase is a full sentence, "it is not much."
history: English link: English is and much are both Germanic. The Latin pieces survived as non- and multi-; Portuguese just says the everyday words in a line: não é muito.

phrases.scene: A small shake of the head over a short pile — not a lot.
phrases.root_image: Latin nōn = not; multum = much, many. Together: not a large amount.
phrases.definition_pt: Uma quantidade pequena: não é uma quantidade grande.
phrases.parts_meaning: não < Latin nōn "not"; muito < Latin multum "much, many"
phrases.origin: The same nōn → não and multum → muito already in earlier lessons, now joined: não muito.
history: English link: English much is Germanic (Old English micel). The Latin multum survived in English as multi-, multiply, multitude. Portuguese keeps one everyday word, muito, and negates it with não.
notes: Não muito answers a question about amount: Você sabe português? — Não muito.

phrases.scene: Inside the guest-house, within its walls.
phrases.root: Latin in + illum + French hôtel ← Latin hospitāle
phrases.root_image: in + o = in the; the hotel is the guest-house (hospitāle). The picture is being inside that house, not just looking at it from the street.
phrases.definition_pt: Dentro do hotel, ou no hotel.
phrases.parts_meaning: no = em + o (in + the, masculine); hotel from French hôtel ← Latin hospitāle (guesthouse)
phrases.origin: no is the regular contraction of em + o, the masculine partner of na (em + a). Portuguese almost always contracts em with the article: no hotel, na carteira, nos Estados Unidos. The noun hotel is the same word as in Lesson 4 (silent h, stress on the end).
history: English link: English in is the Germanic cousin of Latin in / Portuguese em. English says in the hotel or at the hotel, with a separate the; Portuguese fuses in + the into no.
cognates: English in the hotel, at the hotel
notes: no = em + o. Use na before a feminine noun (na carteira, na mala). The h of hotel is silent: no-o-TÉL.

phrases.scene: You scan the room for something upright in its spot, right now.
phrases.root_image: Latin stāre = to stand: something upright in its spot right now.
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta o lugar de alguém ou de alguma coisa agora: “Onde está a mala?”
phrases.literal: "where does it stand?" = where is it (right now)?
phrases.parts_meaning: estar < Latin stāre "to stand"
phrases.origin: stāre → estar (e- added before st-); stat → está.
history: Why English split: English stand is the Germanic cousin of stāre. English uses "is" for location; Portuguese asks "where does it stand?" Ser = be (by essence); estar = stand (for now).
cognates: English stand (Germanic relative), stable, static, station, stay (via Old French ester)
pt_family: estar (to be: state or place now)
notes: E.g. "Onde está o hotel?"
estar = temporary state or location; ser = identity. In speech, está is often shortened to tá: Onde tá?, Tá bom ("OK"). Onde está o hotel?

phrases.scene: You look for the place a stake was driven — fixed, unmoving.
phrases.root: Latin unde + fīgere ‘to fix, fasten’ (via reconstructed *figicāre)
phrases.root_image: Latin fīgere = to fix, fasten, drive in: hammering a nail or stake so something can't move. A crucifix is something fixed to a cross. Ficar comes from a reconstructed Late Latin form, *figicāre.
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta o lugar fixo de alguma coisa: “Onde fica o hotel?”
phrases.literal: "where is it fixed?", which is why it's used for buildings, cities, and things that don't move
phrases.parts_meaning: ficar < Vulgar Latin *figicāre, from Latin fīgere "to fix, fasten"
phrases.origin: *figicāre (reconstructed) → ficar: "to be fixed" → "to remain, stay" → "to be located." Spanish has fincar ("to plant, fix") and Italian ficcare ("to thrust in").
history: Why English split: English got fix from the Latin participle fixus, but for these senses it uses stay (from Old French ester < stāre, "to stand") or "be located."
cognates: English fix, fixture, affix, prefix, suffix, crucifix
pt_family: ficar (to be located; to stay; to become)
culture: ficar is one of Brazil's busiest verbs:
"to stay": Fico aqui = I'll stay here
"to become": ficar triste = to get sad
Fica à vontade = "make yourself at home"
slang ficar com alguém = to hook up or make out casually, without dating
notes: Used for places and other fixed locations.

phrases.scene: An open hand, offered with warmth, asking a kindness in return.
phrases.root_image: Latin favēre = to be well-disposed toward someone, to back them. At Roman rites the call favete linguis ("favor with your tongues") meant "keep holy silence," so no ill-omened word would spoil the ceremony. Favor = goodwill shown.
phrases.definition_pt: Palavras educadas para pedir alguma coisa.
phrases.parts_meaning: por < Latin pro "for, on behalf of" (blended with per "through"); favor < Latin favor "goodwill, support," from favēre "to be well-disposed"
phrases.origin: both words came straight from Latin with little change.
history: Why English split: English kept favor almost unchanged, but its polite word is please, short for "if you please," from Latin placēre (the same root as prazer). English says "if it pleases you"; Portuguese says "as a favor."
notes: Formal signs and polite requests also use por gentileza (see gentil). Faz favor is more typical of Portugal.

phrases.scene: The whole scene is at ease — nothing out of place.
phrases.root_image: Latin tōtus = whole, entire, undivided. English total; in music, tutti = "everyone plays."
phrases.definition_pt: Pergunta e resposta do dia a dia: “Tudo bem?” “Tudo bem!” Também quer dizer “sem problema”.
phrases.parts_meaning: tudo < Latin tōtum "all, the whole"
phrases.origin: tōtum → tudo (intervocalic t → d).
culture: Tudo bem? is the default Brazilian greeting, and Tudo bem is the default answer. Tudo bem? — Tudo bem, e você? Like "How's it going? — Good, you?", it's a ritual, not a real health check.
Variants: Tudo bom? — Tudo ótimo!, Tudo certo?, E aí, tudo bem? ("Hey, all good?"), the casual Beleza? ("Beauty?" = "Cool?").
It also means "It's OK / no problem" after an apology: Desculpa! — Tudo bem.
It often comes with a thumbs up, which Brazilians call joia ("jewel").
notes: Literally "all well."
tudo (everything, unchanging) vs todo/toda ("all, the whole," agrees with its noun).

phrases.scene: A pinch held between two fingers — just that much.
phrases.definition_pt: Uma quantidade pequena: não muito.
phrases.parts_meaning: um < Latin unum "one"; pouco < Latin paucum "few, little"
phrases.origin: unum → um (the n became nasalization); paucum → pouco (au → ou, a regular change).
history: English link: English few is the Germanic relative of Latin paucus (same Indo-European root). Paucity is the learned borrowing.
cognates: paucity (paucus), and English few shares the same ancient root
notes: Falo um pouco de português = "I speak a little Portuguese." Brazilians love the diminutive um pouquinho ("a tiny bit").
